4. *DMA Ingress & Kernel V4L2 Buffer Queue ($t_{\text{DMA}}$):* Scatter-gather DRAM write and driver interrupt $\implies \Delta t_4 =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_dma_str` (illustrative).
5. *Hardware ISP Debayering & Rectification ($t_{\text{ISP}}$):* Dedicated on-chip ISP hardware pass $\implies \Delta t_5 =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_isp_str` (illustrative).
6. *Vision Backbone Tensor Forward Pass ($t_{\text{backbone}}$):* INT8 quantized Vision Transformer on edge NPU $\implies \Delta t_6 =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_backbone_str` (illustrative).
7. *Covariance Packaging & Zero-Copy IPC ($t_{\text{IPC}}$):* Shared-memory circular ring buffer dispatch $\implies \Delta t_7 =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_ipc_str` (illustrative).

**Total Observation Age**:
`{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_display_math`

**Displacement at the Drive Limit**:

At the base's drive limit $v =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.v_str`, holding speed through the age window:
`{python} SensorInformationAge.dx_display_math`

**Systems Impact**: The base covers this distance before the perception record is available at dispatch. Timestamped pose propagation can place the old observation correctly in the current frame, but no later stage returns the distance already traveled.
:::

The seven stages of @tbl-08-latency-budget sum to the dispatch age $t_{\text{age}} =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str`. The existing stopping ledger then adds the active lease and response path of @sec-nervous-cadences:
$$\tau_{\text{delay}} = \underbrace{t_{\text{age}}}_{51.6\,\text{ms}} + \underbrace{t_{\text{lease}} + t_{\text{tick}} + t_{\text{bus}} + t_{\text{act}}}_{82.0\,\text{ms}} = 133.6\,\text{ms}$$

This is a **partial delay ledger**, not yet the capture-to-response bound. The observation ages while the proposer finishes inference, transfers the candidate, and the permission path admits it. Let $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ denote the measured interval from perception dispatch to candidate admission, including those stages and their overlap. Since the active lease begins at admission, the full interval for the stalled-proposer case is the displayed subtotal plus $\Delta_{\text{da}}$. The chapter has not supplied a bound for that interval. Adding a whole inference benchmark independently would also be wrong if part of its work already lies in the vision-backbone stage; the event timestamps must establish the nonoverlapping intervals.

The permission path never reads the image, so it cannot retroactively remove this pipeline age; the age reaches it only through the proposal's evidence epoch. At the `{python} SensorInformationAge.v_str` drive limit, the observation-age term $v\,t_{\text{age}}$ adds `{python} SensorInformationAge.row_age_str` of unmodeled travel to the stopping distance of @eq-body-stopping-distance:
$$d_{\text{stop}} = \underbrace{d_{\text{base}} + d_{\text{lease}}}_{835.5\,\text{mm}} + \underbrace{v \cdot t_{\text{age}}}_{77.4\,\text{mm}} = 912.9\,\text{mm}$$
The partial running total rises from `{python} SensorInformationAge.total_before_str` to `{python} SensorInformationAge.total_after_str`. Its apparent `{python} SensorInformationAge.remaining_str` remainder inside the `{python} SensorInformationAge.d_clear_str` rack-end clear distance must still absorb travel during $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ and the later geometric and trajectory terms. It is not yet available stopping margin. The example sizes a useful perception contribution while identifying the measurement needed before the integrated motion claim can be admitted.

| Stage              |                                       Increment |                                  Serial age after stage | What to verify                          |
|:-------------------|------------------------------------------------:|--------------------------------------------------------:|:----------------------------------------|
| Exposure midpoint  |  `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_exp_half_str` |  `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_exposure_str` | Exposure and row timestamp convention   |
| Rolling readout    |   `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_readout_str` |   `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_readout_str` | Selected row and overlap with streaming |
| Residual transport | `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_transport_str` | `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_transport_str` | Selected sensor mode and host receiver  |
| DMA and queue      |       `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_dma_str` |       `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_dma_str` | Arbitration and queue tail              |
| ISP                |       `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_isp_str` |       `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_isp_str` | Mode and competing jobs                 |
| Vision backbone    |  `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_backbone_str` |  `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_backbone_str` | Workload, clock, thermal state          |
| Dispatch           |       `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_ipc_str` |         **`{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str`** | Capture-to-dispatch age and queue tail  |

: **Serial information-age budget**: The navigation camera's stage increments, assumed nonoverlapping, sum to its observation age. A real pipeline can overlap readout, transfer, and processing, so capture-to-dispatch age requires an end-to-end measurement including queueing tails. Later consumers must add their elapsed post-dispatch interval. {#tbl-08-latency-budget tbl-colwidths="[24,18,20,38]"}

::: {#chk-percep-spatial-info-age .callout-checkpoint title="Information age and the stopping budget"}

Before propagating visual perception into spatial planning, verify your understanding of how pipeline latency creates unmodeled spatial displacement:

- [ ] **Spatial information age**: Can you explain how physical latency from photon exposure to shared-memory dispatch converts directly into unmodeled kinematic displacement, eroding clearance margins before a control policy can react?
- [ ] **Exposure midpoint vs. arrival timestamp**: Can you describe why treating kernel receive timestamps rather than exposure integration midpoints as the capture epoch adds phase lag that can destabilize closed-loop feedback controllers?
- [ ] **Pose propagation from capture time**: Can you explain how propagating the machine's pose forward from an observation's capture time places an old observation correctly in the current frame, and why that propagation cannot return the distance already traveled?
- [ ] **Observation age in the stopping budget**: Can you explain why the observation-age term $v\,t_{\text{age}}$ adds to the stopping distance, and why the permission path, which never reads the image, cannot shorten it?
:::

The serial budget leaves no unassigned waiting time before dispatch. Collecting several frames into one inference batch spends time even before host contention enters the calculation.

### Temporal batching and feedback stability erosion

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-temporal-batching
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TEMPORAL BATCHING ON THE NAVIGATION CAMERA
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The temporal-batching paragraph of @sec-perception-photons-to-claims.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show what a four-frame batch collected across capture times adds
# │          to the navigation camera's observation age.
# │ Show:    16.7 ms frame period at 60 Hz; waits of 50.0, 33.3, and 16.7 ms;
# │          age 51.6 ms -> 101.6 ms, roughly double.
# │ How:     RM.nav_camera.frame_rate; AISLE.perception_age; the oldest of
# │          n frames waits (n - 1) frame periods.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class TemporalBatching:
    """Age added by batching successive navigation-camera frames."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    f_frame = RM.nav_camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond)  # category: derived
    n_batch = 4  # category: illustrative (batch size)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_period = (1 / f_frame).to(millisecond)
    wait_1 = ((n_batch - 1) * t_period).to(millisecond)
    wait_2 = ((n_batch - 2) * t_period).to(millisecond)
    wait_3 = ((n_batch - 3) * t_period).to(millisecond)
    t_age_batched = (t_age + wait_1).to(millisecond)
    ratio = (t_age_batched / t_age).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(f_frame.to(ureg.hertz).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected frame rate: {f_frame}")
    check(abs(wait_1.magnitude - 50.0) < 0.05, f"Unexpected oldest-frame wait: {wait_1}")
    check(abs(t_age_batched.magnitude - 101.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected batched age: {t_age_batched}")
    check(1.8 < ratio < 2.2, f"Prose says batching roughly doubles the age: {ratio}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    f_frame_str = fmt_frequency(f_frame, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    t_period_str = fmt_latency(t_period, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    wait_1_str = fmt_latency(wait_1, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    wait_2_str = fmt_latency(wait_2, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    wait_3_str = fmt_latency(wait_3, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_age_batched_str = fmt_latency(t_age_batched, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

Batching improves accelerator throughput by amortizing work across images, but collecting a batch across successive capture times ages its earliest member. At the navigation camera's `{python} TemporalBatching.f_frame_str` cadence ($T_{\text{sample}} \approx$ `{python} TemporalBatching.t_period_str`), a batch of four consecutive frames holds the first for `{python} TemporalBatching.wait_1_str`, the second and third for `{python} TemporalBatching.wait_2_str` and `{python} TemporalBatching.wait_3_str`, and the last not at all. Adding the oldest frame's wait to the `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.t_age_str` observation age roughly doubles it, to `{python} TemporalBatching.t_age_batched_str`. That exceeds the dispatch-local threshold in @sec-perception-observation-contract, so the frame fails the selected pipeline budget before downstream admission is considered. Images captured together by several cameras may instead be batched only when the batch adds no age beyond the budgeted stages and meets its deadline.

Delay can also make a correction arrive after the motion it was meant to oppose has reversed, so feedback can reinforce the disturbance. Phase margin measures how much additional lag a stable loop can tolerate before that happens. In supporting loop analysis, age spends this margin because a pure delay $t_{\text{age}}$ adds phase lag $\omega t_{\text{age}}$ at frequency $\omega$ without changing gain. Feedback control relies on timely negative feedback to oppose tracking error; when transport and compute latency delay an observation by half an oscillation period, corrective actions arrive in phase with the disturbance rather than opposing it. This phase inversion transforms stabilizing negative feedback into destabilizing positive feedback, driving the robot to chatter, weave across aisles, or oscillate into mechanical resonance. A loop with nominal margin $\text{PM}_{\text{nom}}$ at gain crossover $\omega_c$ therefore exhausts its stability margin once $t_{\text{age}} \ge \text{PM}_{\text{nom}}/\omega_c$, and exposure, processing, transport, permission, and actuator delay all draw on that single ceiling (@sec-appendix-control-zoh). For example, a visual-servoing tracking loop operating at crossover frequency $\omega_c = 10\,\text{rad/s}$ ($\approx 1.6\,\text{Hz}$) with nominal phase margin $\text{PM}_{\text{nom}} = 45^\circ$ ($0.785\,\text{rad}$) has a maximum permissible latency ceiling of $\tau_{\max} = 0.785 / 10 = 78.5\,\text{ms}$. If sensor exposure, transport, and neural inference consume $60\,\text{ms}$, the system depletes over 76 percent of its stability margin before motor commands are dispatched, risking underdamped resonance or boundary chatter.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_phase_margin_erosion_knee.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Knee curve showing phase margin eroding linearly with perception age until reaching instability at seventy-eight milliseconds."}
*Past critical perception age, phase margin erodes to zero, triggering closed-loop instability and chatter.*
:::

The same delay has two consequences: phase lag erodes closed-loop stability margins, while physical travel consumes clearance ($d_{\text{blind}} = v \cdot t_{\text{age}}$). Both checks use the same elapsed interval; counting its two consequences does not justify charging the interval twice in a stopping budget. The capture timestamp, qualified coordinate frame, and error bound make those consequences inspectable. Host ingestion adds another source of waiting: removing a software copy does not remove contention for memory service.

## Ingestion Overhead and Memory Bus Contention {#sec-perception-cost-ingestion}

A common architectural mistake in early physical AI prototypes connects multiple high-resolution cameras via standard USB or Ethernet ports and ingests frames using naive user-space libraries (such as OpenCV's `VideoCapture` or standard ROS image transport). In this naive baseline, every incoming frame is copied from kernel USB request blocks into a driver ring, copied again into user-space process memory, and copied a third time across the PCIe bus into GPU memory. For four 1080p cameras streaming at 60 Hz, this naive pipeline churns through over $1.5\,\text{GB/s}$ of continuous memory copies, adding memory traffic and CPU copying work whose utilization depends on the host, pixel format, and implementation. The data rate alone does not establish CPU saturation or accelerator starvation.

Real-time physical systems avoid this collapse by treating pixel ingestion as a zero-copy DMA\index{Memory!DMA} hardware pipeline. Raw pixel streams arriving over dedicated camera buses bypass CPU copying entirely, writing frames directly into shared physical DRAM before any software thread touches the data. On a shared application processor, however, these camera writes still contend for memory service before inference can read them, and unmanaged bursts can delay host reads or overrun a receiver FIFO and drop a frame.

### MIPI CSI-2 DMA ingress and zero-copy buffers

Once analog-to-digital converters on the sensor die digitize the pixel charges, the frame must travel across a physical interconnect to host memory. Camera streams enter the application processor over the MIPI CSI-2\index{MIPI CSI-2!host ingress} bus.[^fn-hw-mipi-csi]

[^fn-hw-mipi-csi]: **MIPI CSI-2 bus protocol**\index{Hardware!MIPI CSI-2}: CSI-2 transmits serialized pixel streams over D-PHY or C-PHY lanes to a host receiver and DMA controller. It can avoid a network stack, but transport and queueing delay still depend on sensor mode, lane rate, controller, and competing traffic; see @sec-appendix-systems-ipc.

::: {#psp-perception-silicon-ingestion-dataflow-architecture .callout-perspective title="Silicon ingestion dataflow architecture"}
1. **D-PHY / C-PHY physical layer**: Physical lanes serialize pixel packets at the selected sensor and receiver's supported rate; packet headers carry error checks.
2. **System-on-chip (SoC) CSI-2 host controller**: Deserializes byte packets, strips headers, and validates CRC integrity.
3. **Scatter-gather DMA controller**: A dedicated DMA engine transfers pixel byte words directly into DRAM over the internal system interconnect (e.g., AXI crossbar).
4. **Kernel DMA ring buffers**: A Linux `v4l2` driver can map capture buffers into user space.
:::

Once DMA write completion occurs, the kernel driver issues an interrupt.[^fn-hw-v4l2-dma] To eliminate user-space copies, modern embedded Linux systems export DMA buffers directly through the Linux `dma_buf` subsystem. Rather than following the naive three-copy path (Kernel DMA buffer $\to$ User-space buffer $\to$ Pinned host memory $\to$ GPU VRAM), `dma_buf` allows the hardware Image Signal Processor (ISP), CPU, and GPU to import and share the identical physical DRAM pages through system IOMMU page tables. A zero-copy buffer handoff can eliminate bulk CPU copying, but DMA arbitration, synchronization, queueing, and consumer scheduling still contribute to ingestion latency. Format conversion, layout changes, or device alignment constraints can still require a targeted transform, but the bulk pixel payload never traverses the CPU cache hierarchy. On a system without hardware I/O cache coherency, the buffer handoff must synchronize ownership for the actual consumer. CPU access needs the platform's DMA-to-CPU synchronization; accelerator access needs the appropriate device mapping, completion ordering, and cache maintenance for that device. A CPU-side invalidation alone does not establish that an accelerator will read current pixels. These operations belong in the measured ingestion budget.

[^fn-hw-v4l2-dma]: **Video4Linux2 direct memory access**\index{Hardware!V4L2 DMA}: A V4L2 driver may use scatter-gather or physically contiguous DMA storage and expose a capture buffer through `V4L2_MEMORY_MMAP`, which a compatible `dma_buf` importer can share. See @sec-appendix-systems-ipc.

Interface selection trades cable reach and integration flexibility against transport, queueing, and copying costs. MIPI CSI-2 supports direct sensor ingress to the SoC; serializer/deserializer links extend that path across the machine; USB adds a host protocol and driver path whose buffering must be measured. The stage comparison in @fig-08-perception-camera-latency-breakdown helps locate those costs, but an interface name alone does not determine end-to-end latency. Sensor mode, inference workload, and host contention must match the intended deployment.

::: {#fig-08-perception-camera-latency-breakdown fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Illustrative photon-to-actuator latency allocations**: Selected stage durations compare four sensing and interface configurations. The totals are constructed examples, not measured interface bounds or the running machine's stopping budget. Sensor mode, host contention, inference workload, and actuator response must be qualified together; an interface name does not establish determinism." fig-alt="Horizontal stacked bar chart comparing photon-to-actuator latency across four camera interfaces: Neuromorphic Event Camera (11.9 ms), Embedded MIPI CSI-2 (34.6 ms), Automotive GMSL2 (34.8 ms), and Industrial USB 3.0 (58.4 ms). Stacked segments show optical transduction, sensor readout, transport and SerDes, host DMA and ISP, neural inference, planning dispatch, and motor torque rise."}

### Memory bus contention and observation age

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-host-contention-allowance
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HOST CONTENTION THE RENEWAL-JITTER ALLOWANCE TOLERATES
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The memory-bus contention paragraph of @sec-perception-cost-ingestion.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size how much application-processor contention the chunk stream
# │          can absorb before a healthy proposer's renewals leave the lease
# │          rule's jitter allowance, and when a late renewal lapses the lease.
# │ Show:    50 ms chunk period; 5 ms renewal-jitter allowance; a 12.5 percent
# │          stretch of the 40 ms chunk inference; the lease lapses at 10 ms late.
# │ How:     Chunk period from RM.chunk_rate; inference from
# │          RM.chunk_inference_latency; lease from AISLE.t_lease; the 5 ms
# │          allowance is the lease rule's chosen value (@sec-nervous-coupled-budget).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_percent, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class HostContentionAllowance:
    """Application-processor contention absorbed by the lease's renewal-jitter allowance."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    t_infer = RM.chunk_inference_latency.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative (P99 incl. vision)
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen
    t_jitter = 5 * millisecond  # category: chosen (renewal-jitter allowance of the lease rule, @sec-nervous-coupled-budget)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_period = (1 / chunk_rate).to(millisecond)
    t_lapse = (t_lease - t_period).to(millisecond)
    stretch = (t_jitter / t_infer).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_period.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected chunk period: {t_period}")
    check(abs(t_jitter.to(millisecond).magnitude - 5.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected renewal-jitter allowance: {t_jitter}")
    check(t_period + t_jitter < t_lease, "Lease rule: chunk period plus jitter must be shorter than the lease")
    check(abs(t_lapse.magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected lapse point: {t_lapse}")
    check(t_infer < t_period, "Chunk inference must fit inside one chunk period")
    check(abs(stretch - 0.125) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected inference stretch: {stretch}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_period_str = fmt_latency(t_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_jitter_str = fmt_latency(t_jitter.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_infer_str = fmt_latency(t_infer, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lapse_str = fmt_latency(t_lapse, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    stretch_pct_str = fmt_percent(stretch, precision=1)
```

The raw rates of the machine's navigation and wrist cameras are sized in \ref{nbk-data-ingestion-bandwidth-storage-budgets-multi-camera}. When the perception stack reads those frames, copies or transforms intermediate buffers, and the accelerator reads weights and writes activations, the memory controller carries several times that ingress rate. Even that multiple sits well inside the memory system's peak bandwidth when averaged over a second.

Average bandwidth does not determine the latency of one read. On edge robotics SoCs such as the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, the CPU cluster, deep learning accelerator (DLA), GPU, and CSI-2 DMA engines share a single physical DRAM bus (Unified Memory Architecture, or UMA). Synchronized cameras concentrate their DMA writes into sharp bursts, saturating memory channels and causing widespread DRAM bank conflicts. When multiple cameras dump un-cached raster lines across the system crossbar simultaneously, they continuously open and close DRAM page buffers across active banks. If the neural accelerator attempts to stream transformer model weights and intermediate activation tensors during this exact window, memory controller arbitration stalls accelerator read requests behind high-priority sensor DMA streams. These memory read stalls introduce pipeline bubbles in hardware tensor cores, stretching neural inference latency by 10 to 15 percent and creating severe tail latency spikes ($P_{99}$ jitter).

On the mobile manipulator, this burst lands only on the application processor. The permission path runs on its own microcontroller and reads its state from its own isolated SRAM, so a memory burst cannot stretch its safety tick\index{Bus jitter}, and the shared-die placement that would expose those reads is the one @sec-placement-resource-contention rejects. The burst reaches the permission path only as the age of the frame a proposal is built on or the lateness of the renewal the chunk policy sends, and the two have different allowances. A frame that waits behind camera and accelerator traffic reaches dispatch older than the budgeted stages, and the refusal threshold of @sec-perception-observation-contract leaves no slack above them, so every proposal built on that frame is refused.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_dma_ingress_slack_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Budget envelope showing four-camera 4K DMA burst exhausting 850-microsecond timing slack."}
*A rejected shared-memory placement: camera bursts can exhaust a control loop's slack when both compete for the same memory. The running machine isolates its permission loop.*
:::

A chunk whose inference waits behind the same traffic renews the lease late, and there the lease rule of @sec-nervous-coupled-budget leaves `{python} HostContentionAllowance.t_jitter_str` of renewal jitter above the `{python} HostContentionAllowance.t_period_str` chunk period. Host contention may therefore stretch the chunk policy's `{python} HostContentionAllowance.t_infer_str` inference by at most `{python} HostContentionAllowance.stretch_pct_str` percent, and by less in practice, because the same allowance also holds the proposer's own jitter and the jitter of the board-level link to the microcontroller (@sec-placement-isolation-decisions). A renewal `{python} HostContentionAllowance.t_lapse_str` late lets the lease lapse and stops the machine. With the stated isolation, age checks, and feasible fallback intact, excess contention costs availability: the permission path refuses delay outside the qualified budget. That conclusion depends on those premises, including continued access to valid local evidence.

How long a burst holds the bus also matters to the camera interface itself. Ingest engines utilize direct memory access ring buffers with double or triple buffering to decouple arrival interrupts from consumer reading threads. If host memory bus contention delays DMA completion beyond what the CSI-2 receiver hardware FIFO can buffer, the receiver suffers an overrun and silently drops the frame. A dropped frame doubles the effective observation interval between samples, and downstream state observers must treat the missing update as an age or sequence fault rather than assuming that fresh scene geometry will arrive on schedule.

The hardware mechanisms governing frame delivery (DMA rings, IOMMU mappings, and DRAM arbitration) are treated by @hennessy2019computer and @bryant2015computer. For this chapter's decision, the quantity that matters is capture-to-consumer age and its tail under the intended camera workload.

An on-time frame answers only when the scene was sampled. Where the objects in it are, and how far that estimate can be trusted, is a separate question, and the error in that answer is spent from the same clearance.

## Spatial Error and Clearance Bounds {#sec-perception-error-clearance}

When perception places a rack upright a few centimeters farther from the base's path than it actually stands, the base plans its pass with those centimeters missing from the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.side_clearance_str` side clearance it keeps from the racks, and no stage of the pipeline decided to spend them. Once downstream control logic uses an estimated coordinate to authorize motion, a spatial error becomes a physical displacement, spent out of the same clearance that keeps the machine off the obstacle. Transforming a sensor observation into a clearance claim requires **metric grounding**\index{Metric grounding!definition}, which maps raw detector measurements into geometric space. This grounding relies on unprojecting two-dimensional sensor coordinates into three dimensions, an inversion that assumes known optics, rigid mounting, and predictable surface properties.

The mathematical principles of projection and triangulation [@hartley2003multiple; @szeliski2022computer] govern how measurement noise converts into spatial displacement. In two-view streaming perception, two cameras with optical centers $\mathbf{C}_1, \mathbf{C}_2$ observe a physical 3D scene point $\mathbf{P}$. The baseline vector $\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ connecting $\mathbf{C}_1$ and $\mathbf{C}_2$, along with the point $\mathbf{P}$, forms the **epipolar plane**\index{Epipolar geometry!epipolar plane}. The intersection of the baseline with each image plane defines the **epipoles** $\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2$.

For image coordinates $\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2$ expressed in homogeneous pixel coordinates, the rigid spatial transformation $(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}) \in \text{SE}(3)$ relating the camera frames establishes the fundamental **epipolar constraint**\index{Epipolar constraint!definition}:
$$\mathbf{x}_2^\top \mathbf{F} \, \mathbf{x}_1 = 0$$
where $\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{K}_2^{-\top} \mathbf{E} \, \mathbf{K}_1^{-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ is the **Fundamental matrix**\index{Fundamental matrix}, and $\mathbf{E} = [\mathbf{t}]_\times \mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ is the **Essential matrix**\index{Essential matrix} (with $[\mathbf{t}]_\times$ denoting the skew-symmetric matrix of the baseline translation). The vector $\mathbf{l}_2 = \mathbf{F} \mathbf{x}_1$ defines the **epipolar line** in the second image; any physical correspondence $\mathbf{x}_2$ must lie strictly along $\mathbf{l}_2$.

In a calibrated **rectified stereo rig**\index{Stereo rectification!epipolar lines}, both images are digitally warped onto a common virtual image plane parallel to the baseline ($\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I}$, $\mathbf{t} = [b, 0, 0]^\top$). Rectification forces epipolar lines to be exactly parallel and collinear with horizontal scanlines ($y_1 = y_2$). In modern neural stereo networks (such as RAFT-Stereo or CoEx), this geometric transformation collapses a computationally intractable two-dimensional correspondence search into an efficient one-dimensional correlation volume evaluated strictly along the same horizontal scanline: disparity is simply $d = u_1 - u_2$, recovering metric depth $z = \frac{f b}{d}$.

When mechanical vibration, chassis twist, or thermal expansion induces uncalibrated relative pitch or roll between cameras, or when rolling-shutter readout shears scanlines during robot rotation, the true physical correspondence shifts vertically off the horizontal epipolar line ($\Delta y \neq 0$). The 1D correlation cost volume fails or locks onto spurious texture matches across adjacent rows, producing severe triangulation outliers. Differentiating the unprojection $z = \frac{f b}{d}$ with respect to disparity gives a negative signed derivative; its magnitude yields the small-error relation (@eq-percep-stereo-uncertainty):
$$|\delta z| \approx \frac{z^2}{f b} |\delta d|$$ {#eq-percep-stereo-uncertainty}
where $\delta d$ is a small disparity error.[^fn-math-inverse-depth] If $\delta d$ denotes a disparity standard deviation $\sigma_d$, first-order propagation gives $\sigma_z\approx z^2\sigma_d/(fb)$. Doubling range quadruples this modeled standard deviation at fixed $f$, $b$, and $\sigma_d$. For distant landmarks, an estimator instead carries depth as inverse depth $\rho = 1/z = d / (f b)$. Differentiating with respect to disparity yields:
$$\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial d} = \frac{1}{f b} = \text{constant}$$
Because this derivative is independent of distance, measurement errors in disparity map linearly into inverse depth ($\delta \rho = \frac{1}{f b} \delta d$). This linear mapping provides **inverse-depth metric grounding**\index{Inverse-depth metric grounding!definition}, which can improve numerical conditioning for distant landmarks when the disparity-error model is appropriate. It does not eliminate mismatch outliers or guarantee estimator stability. A pulsed time-of-flight sensor instead estimates $z=c\Delta t/2$; its range error depends on its timing and detection mechanism and may be approximately flat over a specified operating region.

This quadratic depth error growth poses an acute challenge when compounded with observation latency tails. While image serialization, DMA ingress, and stereo matching execute across observation age $t_{\text{age}}$, the robot continues moving toward the obstacle by $\Delta x = v \cdot t_{\text{age}}$. If the perception pipeline experiences an inference latency tail—stretching $t_{\text{age}}$ from $51.6\,\text{ms}$ to $120\,\text{ms}$ under memory bus contention—the physical gap to the obstacle closes by $180\,\text{mm}$ before the disparity map is even dispatched. Compounding this unmodeled physical displacement with the quadratic depth dispersion $\delta z \propto z^2$ rapidly consumes the vehicle's safe stopping margin unless downstream planners enforce an expanded clearance inset.

[^fn-math-inverse-depth]: **Inverse-depth parameterization**\index{Mathematics!inverse-depth}: In visual state estimation, parameterizing 3D landmarks by inverse depth ($\rho = 1/z$) makes small disparity perturbations linear in inverse depth. Approximate Gaussian behavior follows only if the disparity residual model supports it; correspondence outliers remain outliers. Under inverse depth, points at optical infinity ($z \to \infty$) exhibit finite variance ($\rho \to 0$). For the rigorous derivation and mathematical formulation, see @sec-appendix-ml-spatial.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-stereo-depth-error
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STEREO DEPTH-ERROR SCALE AND BASELINE THERMAL BIAS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The stereo worked example of @sec-perception-error-clearance and
# │          the thermal-expansion footnote of @sec-perception-observation-contract.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show how the one-sigma stereo depth scale grows with squared range,
# │          why adding it to a clearance kept along the viewing ray does not
# │          give an inset, and
# │          what an unmodeled baseline change does to depth at long range.
# │ Show:    sigma_z 12.5 mm at 2 m and 312.5 mm at 10 m; a 150 mm ray clearance plus
# │          one sigma 162.5 mm and 462.5 mm; 10 mm depth bias at 20 m.
# │ How:     sigma_z = z^2 sigma_d / (f b); |dz| = z |db| / b.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, check

class StereoDepthError:
    """One-sigma stereo depth scale on an illustrative rig, and baseline thermal bias."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    b = 0.20 * meter  # category: illustrative (stereo baseline)
    f_px = 800.0  # category: illustrative (focal length, pixels)
    sigma_d_px = 0.5  # category: illustrative (disparity standard deviation, pixels)
    z_near = 2.0 * meter  # category: illustrative
    z_far = 10.0 * meter  # category: illustrative
    db = 0.1 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative (unmodeled baseline change)
    z_thermal = 20.0 * meter  # category: illustrative
    c_ray = 150.0 * ureg.millimeter  # category: illustrative (clearance kept along the viewing ray)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    sigma_z_near = (z_near**2 * sigma_d_px / (f_px * b)).to(ureg.millimeter)
    sigma_z_far = (z_far**2 * sigma_d_px / (f_px * b)).to(ureg.millimeter)
    naive_near = (c_ray + sigma_z_near).to(ureg.millimeter)
    naive_far = (c_ray + sigma_z_far).to(ureg.millimeter)
    dz_thermal = (z_thermal * db / b).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(sigma_z_near.magnitude - 12.5) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected near sigma_z: {sigma_z_near}")
    check(abs(sigma_z_far.magnitude - 312.5) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected far sigma_z: {sigma_z_far}")
    check(abs(sigma_z_far / sigma_z_near - 25.0) < 1e-9, "Depth scale must grow with squared range")
    check(abs(dz_thermal.magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected thermal depth bias: {dz_thermal}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    b_str = fmt_length(b, unit=meter, precision=2)
    f_px_str = fmt(f_px, precision=0)
    sigma_d_px_str = fmt(sigma_d_px, precision=1)
    z_near_str = fmt_length(z_near, unit=meter, precision=0)
    z_far_str = fmt_length(z_far, unit=meter, precision=0)
    sigma_z_near_str = fmt_length(sigma_z_near, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    sigma_z_far_str = fmt_length(sigma_z_far, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    c_ray_str = fmt_length(c_ray, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    naive_near_str = fmt_length(naive_near, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    naive_far_str = fmt_length(naive_far, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    db_str = fmt_length(db, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    z_thermal_str = fmt_length(z_thermal, unit=meter, precision=0)
    dz_thermal_str = fmt_length(dz_thermal, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
```

To quantify the geometry, assume an illustrative stereo pair (the navigation camera alone recovers only the bearing ray of @eq-percep-bearing-ray) with $b =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.b_str`, $f =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.f_px_str` px, and disparity standard deviation $\sigma_d =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.sigma_d_px_str` px over the tested range. First-order propagation gives $\sigma_z =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.sigma_z_near_str` at `{python} StereoDepthError.z_near_str` and $\sigma_z =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.sigma_z_far_str` at `{python} StereoDepthError.z_far_str` (@fig-08-depth-uncertainty-clearance). Those are **one-standard-deviation scales**, not clearance insets or 99th-percentile bounds. A usable inset requires a tail quantile of the *full spatial residual*, calibrated on the intended sensor, range, texture, motion, and lighting conditions, with systematic bias and missed detections handled separately.

A pervasive trap in visual estimation is assuming that measurement errors follow a nominal Gaussian distribution where a $3\sigma$ gate bounds 99.7 percent of all errors. In physical vision, disparity estimation relies on matching pixel patches across stereo images. When scenes contain repetitive textures (such as corrugated warehouse siding), specular reflections from polished concrete floors, or partial occlusions along object silhouettes, correspondence matching produces catastrophic multimodal outliers rather than Gaussian scatter. In real-world robotic environments, 2 to 5 percent of stereo returns represent complete mismatch outliers lying dozens of standard deviations from the true surface. Relying on Gaussian $3\sigma$ bounds without robust loss formulations (such as Huber or Tukey loss) or heavy-tailed empirical quantile validation allows these gross outliers to distort the state estimate, compromising physical clearance. A `{python} StereoDepthError.c_ray_str` clearance kept along the viewing ray to an obstacle therefore cannot be widened to a valid inset of `{python} StereoDepthError.naive_near_str` or `{python} StereoDepthError.naive_far_str` merely by adding one $\sigma_z$. Speed must be reduced or the proposal refused whenever the validated range-error and stopping margins do not fit.

### Clearance inset margins and transform chain propagation

Spatial error extends beyond the sensor optical frame. To govern motion, the estimated point must propagate through coordinate transformations to the robot base frame and the end effector. The mechanics of rigid body transformations\index{Rigid body transformations} and SE(3) kinematic frame composition\index{SE(3) kinematics} are standard results treated by Craig [@craig2005introduction] as well as @lynch2017modern. Each link in this transform chain contributes scale errors, mounting calibration drift, joint encoder quantization, and mechanical compliance under load (such as a robot arm sagging slightly under gravity). Lever-arm effects amplify a small angular twist at the sensor mount linearly over distance, sweeping projected coordinates across a wide arc. If the navigation camera's extrinsic calibration shifts by $\theta =$ `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.theta_ext_str` rad against the chassis, the lateral error $\delta x \approx z\theta$ at $z =$ `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.z_ext_str` is `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.dx_ext_str`, equal in size to the whole `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.delta_loc_str` localization allowance $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ that the stopping budget holds along the direction of travel. The comparison is one of scale, not allocation. The allowance carries small validated residuals, such as the clock-conversion travel of @sec-perception-observation-contract, and a shift that matches it alone is a calibration failure the consumer must refuse through the calibration validity check rather than absorb. When combined with quadratic depth uncertainty, the total spatial error vector $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\text{spatial}}$ at long range is dominated by depth along the optical axis and angular lever-arm effects orthogonal to it.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Spatial covariance envelopes inflate the forward-invariant safety barrier sets derived in @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission.
:::

Every physical safety barrier operates by defending a geometric boundary around the machine. For position error vector $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\text{spatial}}$, the triangle inequality gives a conservative relation between nominal and true clearance:
$$C_{\text{true}} \ge C_{\text{nominal}} - \|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\text{spatial}}\|$$
For a validated 99th-percentile norm-error quantile, the permission path can choose an **inset clearance**\index{Inset clearance!definition} $C_{\text{inset}}$ (@eq-percep-clearance-inset):
$$C_{\text{inset}} = C_{\text{safe}} + \|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\text{spatial}}\|_{P_{99}}$$ {#eq-percep-clearance-inset}
Here $C_{\text{safe}}$ is the physical clearance the motion must keep, such as the base's side clearance, and the quantile must come from a specified, checked residual distribution for the full spatial error, including calibration bias. Even then it leaves a 1 percent tail under the test distribution; only a justified hard bound on the relevant error, a feasible stopping path, and a permission response within the remaining delay budget would close it. @Fig-08-depth-uncertainty-clearance shows how stereo's growing depth-error scale can require a larger inset at longer range.

::: {#fig-08-depth-uncertainty-clearance fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Depth error scale and clearance insets**: (A) A stereo one-standard-deviation depth scale grows with squared range for fixed disparity spread; a qualified time-of-flight sensor can be flatter. (B) A validated 99th-percentile *norm-error* quantile enlarges the nominal clearance inset and leaves a residual tail and bias risk. Attribution: Book geometric error analysis, CC BY 4.0." fig-alt="Panel (a) compares a stereo depth standard deviation that rises quadratically with range with a flatter qualified time-of-flight error curve. Panel (b) shows a robot, obstacle, and an inset based on a separately validated 99th-percentile spatial-error quantile, with a residual tail beyond it."}
![](images/svg/fig08_depth_uncertainty_clearance.svg){width="95%"}
:::

Because clearance depends on propagated error, downstream planners and the permission path cannot consume raw coordinate tuples. A covariance $\mathbf{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ alone does not say whether a $10\text{ mm}$ or $500\text{ mm}$ clearance inset is warranted; that takes an independently validated tail or hard bound.

When spatial error is qualified, the permission path can expand the clearance inset, trading speed or workspace for separation. Downstream deterministic safety filters (such as the Control Barrier Functions derived in @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission) enforce forward invariance against this expanded boundary $C_{\text{inset}}$, preserving the physical clearance buffer against sensing and calibration error. A textureless wall, glare, or lost calibration can invalidate that qualification without making a numerical variance literally infinite. The permission path must then refuse motion that depends on the affected claim and select a feasible fallback.

On every frame the producer builds a spatial claim in a fixed order, and any step can end it. It first converts the capture timestamp to the consumer's clock with a bounded synchronization error and computes $t_{\text{age}}$; if age plus clock uncertainty exceeds the refusal threshold, it marks the observation stale, and proposals that need it are refused. At admission and subsequent ticks, the permission path computes the current evidence age from capture time; the dispatch threshold is not the current-age threshold (@sec-perception-observation-contract). For a fresh observation, the producer unprojects each pixel measurement into optical coordinates with a sensor covariance,[^fn-math-unprojection-covariance] and carries point and covariance into the body frame by first-order SE(3) error propagation\index{SE(3) kinematics!error propagation} through the calibrated extrinsics at capture. A consumer that predicts forward must attach its motion-model uncertainty without changing the evidence epoch. Validated residuals, including bias, then set the inset radius, and when no valid bound remains, the affected motion is refused. What leaves perception is a claim $(\mathbf{p}_{\text{body}}, \mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{body}}, C_{\text{inset}}, t_{\text{age}})$, not a bare coordinate.

[^fn-math-unprojection-covariance]: **Metric unprojection and covariance propagation**\index{Mathematics!covariance propagation}: First-order propagation maps measurement covariance to $\mathbf{\Sigma}_c = \mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{meas}}\mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}}^\top$ and then to $\mathbf{\Sigma}_b = \mathbf{R}_{bc}\mathbf{\Sigma}_c\mathbf{R}_{bc}^\top + \mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{ext}}$. Its largest eigenvalue gives a principal variance scale, **not** a 99th-percentile error radius. A quantile requires an assumed and calibrated error distribution, including bias; see @sec-appendix-systems-vision.

### Learned scene representations and depth estimation

Open-vocabulary perception adds a learned semantic layer above metric sensing, built from **3D vision foundation models**\index{3D vision foundation models}. A self-supervised backbone such as DINOv2 [@oquab2023dinov2] yields dense patch features, a promptable segmenter such as SAM [@kirillov2023segment] yields class-agnostic instance masks, and systems such as ConceptGraphs [@kuwajerwala2024conceptgraphs; @jatavallabhula2023conceptfusion] and Hydra [@hughes2022hydra] lift those masks and features through calibrated depth, extrinsics, and odometry into an **object-centric 3D scene graph**\index{Object-centric 3D scene graph!definition} whose nodes carry a centroid, a spatial covariance, and a text-aligned embedding.

The semantic layer identifies candidate objects and contacts. The metric layer must still establish their geometry. Point clouds supply measured surface samples; missing samples do not establish free space. Occupancy and distance fields retain geometric evidence for repeated queries, while Gaussian scene models optimize appearance and require separate geometric qualification before collision use. @Sec-memory selects these persistent representations by the query and its resource budget; @sec-appendix-ml-voxels supplies voxel update equations and @sec-appendix-ml-3dgs supplies Gaussian parameterization. Those storage mechanisms do not change the observation's capture time or turn a learned score into an error bound.

Lifting 2D pixel features into 3D metric space requires combining 2D token embeddings with per-pixel depth distributions. In deep monocular depth networks (such as Depth Anything, MiDaS, or metric depth transformers), models predict dense depth maps from monocular cues. However, single-view depth estimation is inherently ill-posed due to projective scale ambiguity: an infinite family of physical 3D objects with different scales and distances project to identical pixel arrays. Relative-depth models may output scale- or affine-ambiguous predictions, whose conversion to metric depth requires calibration, represented here by $z_{\text{metric}} = s \cdot z_{\text{pred}} + t$ when the model uses that parameterization. Metric-trained heads can directly predict depth in meters, but their units do not certify their error. Either kind of model requires residual validation and can fail silently on unusual geometries, novel textures, or optical illusions (such as a 2D photograph printed on a flat surface).

In bird's-eye-view (BEV) architectures such as Lift-Splat-Shoot [@philion2020lift] (developed in @sec-appendix-ml-bev-lifting), the network predicts a categorical probability distribution over discrete depth bins along each viewing ray. Each 2D feature token is cast outward along its optical sightline ray and 'splatted' into discrete 3D spatial voxel cells weighted by these predicted depth probabilities, transforming disembodied image embeddings into an explicit 3D volumetric representation. Crucially, the resulting spatial uncertainty ellipsoid deforms non-linearly under perspective unprojection through the unprojection Jacobian $\mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{p}_{\text{cartesian}}}{\partial [u, v, z]^\top}$ (@eq-percep-unproj-covariance):
$$\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{cartesian}} = \mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}} \mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{ray}} \mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}}^\top$$ {#eq-percep-unproj-covariance}
While transverse spatial standard deviation expands linearly with range ($\sigma_\perp \approx \frac{z}{f} \sigma_{\text{px}}$), stereo radial depth standard deviation expands quadratically ($\sigma_z \approx \frac{z^2}{f b} \sigma_d$). This perspective unprojection transforms near-field circular uncertainty disks into highly eccentric, needle-shaped ellipsoids oriented along the camera's sightline, with extreme radial dispersion at long ranges that must be bound before downstream safety filters can certify clearance.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-encoder-rate
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FOUNDATION-MODEL ENCODER AT CAMERA RATE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The learned-features paragraph of @sec-perception-error-clearance.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that a heavy encoder at the navigation camera's frame rate
# │          exceeds the application processor's peak dense FP16 rate.
# │ Show:    3 TFLOP per frame at 60 Hz = 180 TFLOP/s against 43 TFLOP/s.
# │ How:     Assumed encoder cost; RM.nav_camera.frame_rate; published Jetson
# │          AGX Orin dense FP16 peak (registry carries only INT8; LOAD here
# │          until an add-only precision_flops fp16 entry lands).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_flops, fmt_frequency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class EncoderAtCameraRate:
    """Sustained throughput a per-frame foundation encoder would need."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    encoder_tflop = 3.0  # category: illustrative (assumed encoder cost per frame, TFLOP)
    f_frame = RM.nav_camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet
    orin_fp16_dense_tflops = 43.0  # category: datasheet (NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin technical brief, dense FP16 peak)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    required_tflops = encoder_tflop * f_frame.to(ureg.hertz).magnitude
    shortfall = required_tflops / orin_fp16_dense_tflops

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(required_tflops - 180.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected required throughput: {required_tflops}")
    check(shortfall > 1.0, "Prose says the encoder cannot run at camera rate even at peak")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    encoder_tflop_str = fmt_flops(encoder_tflop * TFLOP, unit=TFLOP, precision=0)
    f_frame_str = fmt_frequency(f_frame, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    required_tflops_str = fmt(required_tflops, precision=0)
    orin_fp16_dense_tflops_str = fmt(orin_fp16_dense_tflops, precision=0)
```

These features spend a compute and age budget [@williams2009roofline]. An assumed `{python} EncoderAtCameraRate.encoder_tflop_str` encoder at the navigation camera's `{python} EncoderAtCameraRate.f_frame_str` frame rate would require `{python} EncoderAtCameraRate.required_tflops_str` TFLOP/s of sustained useful throughput before preprocessing or memory traffic, while NVIDIA lists up to `{python} EncoderAtCameraRate.orin_fp16_dense_tflops_str` dense FP16 TFLOP/s for the Jetson AGX Orin in its [technical brief](https://www.nvidia.com/content/dam/en-zz/Solutions/gtcf21/jetson-orin/nvidia-jetson-agx-orin-technical-brief.pdf), a peak arithmetic rate rather than sustained model throughput. The encoder cannot run at camera rate on that processor even at the arithmetic ceiling, so one candidate design is a **multi-rate hierarchy**\index{Multi-rate hierarchy!definition}. In that alternative, metric ingress on the application processor\index{Microprocessor} turns the camera's DMA buffers\index{MIPI CSI-2!DMA buffers} into obstacle points and occupancy grids at $30\text{--}60\text{ Hz}$ without the heavy backbone, and the foundation models update the scene graph's semantic nodes on keyframes at $1\text{--}5\text{ Hz}$. A slow semantic update is admissible only when fresh metric sensing and the permission path hold the physical margin between updates.

Because the depth-bin distributions produced by learned lifting stages are uncalibrated model scores rather than certified metric error bounds, the clearance inset of @eq-percep-clearance-inset cannot rest on learned depth alone. Downstream safety enforcers require continuous validation against calibrated active ranging sensors or stereo disparity.

::: {#psp-perception-metric-veto-invariant .callout-perspective title="The metric veto invariant"}
**Safety is an invariant of metric clearance, not semantic understanding.** When a slow 2 Hz vision-language foundation model classifies a pathway as "clear aisle" or dismisses an object as a harmless shadow, but a fast 60 Hz depth sensor or occupancy grid detects a physical obstacle return within the stopping envelope, the permission path must honor the qualified occupied-region evidence rather than let semantic confidence erase it. The permission path halts or slows the machine regardless of the semantic model's high confidence. Semantic models propose high-level task goals; qualified metric sensing supplies clearance evidence to the permission path. Neither sensor pipeline itself owns actuator authority.
:::

### Multi-object tracking and temporal data association {#sec-perception-tracking-association}

A fresh occupied-region claim can constrain motion before the system knows which object produced it. Persistent identity serves another purpose: joining detections across frames lets the planner estimate velocity and anticipate a crossing. Detection flicker makes that association uncertain, but withholding occupancy until identity is confirmed would create an avoidable interval of blindness.

The interface therefore separates immediate geometric evidence from a **tracking-by-detection** hypothesis. The tracker associates detections, estimates motion, and carries uncertainty; @sec-memory owns persistence and expiry through missing observations. The following state equations describe the additional information a confirmed track can supply, not a prerequisite for acting on an obstacle return.

Each active track $i$ maintains a kinematic state vector $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_t = [\hat{\mathbf{p}}_t^\top, \hat{\mathbf{v}}_t^\top]^\top$ and error covariance $\mathbf{P}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{6\times6}$, propagated forward in time by a kinematic transition matrix $\mathbf{F}$ and process noise covariance $\mathbf{Q}$:
$$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t|t-1} = \mathbf{F}\,\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t-1|t-1}, \quad \mathbf{P}_{t|t-1} = \mathbf{F}\,\mathbf{P}_{t-1|t-1}\mathbf{F}^\top + \mathbf{Q}$$ {#eq-percep-track-propagation}
When a new frame delivers $M$ candidate detections $\{\mathbf{z}_{t, j}\}_{j=1}^M$, the tracker must resolve **data association**—deciding which detection belongs to which track. To prevent associating spurious sensor noise or distant objects, the tracker computes the squared Mahalanobis distance $d_{M, ij}^2$ between detection $\mathbf{z}_{t, j}$ and the predicted measurement $\mathbf{H}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t|t-1}$:
$$d_{M, ij}^2 = (\mathbf{z}_{t, j} - \mathbf{H}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t|t-1})^\top \mathbf{S}_{ij}^{-1} (\mathbf{z}_{t, j} - \mathbf{H}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t|t-1})$$ {#eq-percep-mahalanobis-gate}
where $\mathbf{S}_{ij} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{P}_{t|t-1}\mathbf{H}^\top + \mathbf{R}_j$ is the innovation covariance and $\mathbf{R}_j$ is the measurement error covariance. A **validation gate** evaluates @eq-percep-mahalanobis-gate and rejects any pairing where $d_{M, ij}^2 > \gamma_{\text{gate}}$, where a chi-squared threshold $\chi_3^2(1 - \alpha)$ has its nominal interpretation only under the assumed residual model. Empirical association errors require separate validation. For all gated pairs, the tracker constructs an assignment cost matrix $\mathbf{C}_{ij} = d_{M, ij}^2$ and solves the optimal global bipartite matching via the Hungarian algorithm [@kuhn1955hungarian] or Jonker-Volgenant assignment [@bewley2016simple], enforcing one-to-one assignment among the candidate pairings; it does not prove that the association is physically correct.

One common track lifecycle distinguishes three states:

1. **Tentative state**: Unassociated detections spawn tentative tracks. Because false detections arise frequently from specular reflections, dust, or lens flare, the identity remains tentative until an $M$-of-$N$ confirmation rule is met. Fresh occupied-region evidence remains visible to clearance consumers during confirmation. If a downstream decision requires confirmed identity or velocity, its detection delay must include that confirmation interval; the single-frame waterfall cannot stand in for it.
2. **Confirmed state**: Once confirmed, the track publishes its full state estimate $(\text{ID}_i, \hat{\mathbf{p}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{v}}_i, \mathbf{P}_i)$ to the planning and intent layers. Measurement updates refine the state mean and contract the covariance via optimal gain corrections.
3. **Coasting state (occlusion)**: When an obstacle passes behind a warehouse shelf or is occluded by another actor, detection fails. Rather than terminating the track immediately, the system transitions the track to a coasting state. During coasting, state is propagated strictly via the motion model $\mathbf{F}$ in @eq-percep-track-propagation, and process noise $\mathbf{Q}$ adds uncertainty without a new measurement to constrain it. Downstream planners must treat coasting obstacles with expanding clearance margins. If no matching detection arrives within a timeout horizon $T_{\text{lost}}$, the identity track terminates. Termination does not establish that its last occupied region is free; memory must retain the appropriate unknown-space constraint.

When a decision requires tracked motion, perception also emits an auditable **dynamic track manifest** $[(\text{ID}_k, \hat{\mathbf{p}}_k, \hat{\mathbf{v}}_k, \mathbf{P}_k, t_{\text{last}}, \text{state})]$. Downstream intent filters in @sec-intent-admissible-goal-sets consume these velocities and covariances to establish dynamic exclusion cones, while safety enforcers in @sec-enforcement evaluate stopping clearance against moving targets.

Every bound in this section, metric, learned, or temporal, assumes that the sensor behaves as calibrated. Propagation bounds the error of a sensor working as modeled; it says nothing about a sensor that has stopped working that way while still delivering frames at its nominal rate.

## Perception Failure Modes and Sensor Degradation {#sec-perception-failure-modes}

The navigation camera can fail in two ways that look nothing alike to its consumer. If its serializer link loses lock, the driver raises an error and the frame never arrives. If light through an open dock door saturates the lens as the base turns into an aisle, the camera delivers a complete frame at its nominal rate in which the rack end is a patch of saturated white. Perception failures divide along exactly this line into two operational classes. **Detectable faults**\index{Detectable faults} occur when the physical sensor or the communication transport reports an explicit error condition. A serializer-deserializer link drops a lock (losing clock synchronization), a cyclical redundancy check detects a corrupted payload, a frame buffer overflows, or a transport bus times out. These failures are straightforward to handle since the hardware driver asserts an error flag at the ingestion boundary. Downstream consumers register the missing frame and invalidate stale state estimates, and once the evidence age exceeds its budget the permission path refuses and moves the machine to a validated fallback. In contrast, **silent failures**\index{Silent failure!definition} occur when the sensor hardware and transport pipeline function without error, delivering a fully populated, structurally valid tensor whose numerical values misrepresent the physical world.

Physical degradation of the optical channel is a common source of silent error.[^fn-hw-lidar-drift] When direct sunlight enters an optical aperture, incident photons exceed the physical charge capacity (the "full-well capacity") of the CMOS photodiodes, clamping pixel intensities at their maximum quantization limit (clipping the image to pure white) across large patches of the array. This **dynamic range saturation**\index{Dynamic range saturation} destroys local spatial gradients. Feature extractors, optical flow estimators, and disparity matching algorithms fail because mathematical optimization on a uniform flat field yields zero information, yet the driver emits a valid frame at nominal line rate. Low-light environments introduce the opposite failure mode. As ambient illumination drops, the discrete, random arrival of individual photons (**photon shot noise**\index{Photon shot noise}) and the intrinsic electrical fluctuations of the sensor's amplifier (**sensor read noise**\index{Sensor read noise}) dominate the measurement. The signal-to-noise ratio collapses, causing downstream neural networks to extract geometric features from random noise fluctuations rather than physical scene boundaries. Environmental contaminants on the protective lens or dome window (such as water droplets, airborne dust, or mud splatters) act as irregular refractive elements and optical low-pass filters. They attenuate contrast, distort spatial geometry, and obscure obstacles while the transport bus continues to operate without asserting a single fault flag.

[^fn-hw-lidar-drift]: **Lidar range walk and detector blooming**\index{Hardware!lidar range walk}: Analogous silent degradation occurs in active time-of-flight lidar receivers utilizing Avalanche Photodiodes (APDs) or Single-Photon Avalanche Diodes (SPADs). When an emitted laser pulse reflects off a retroreflective surface, intense return energy drives the photodetector into non-linear charge saturation, accelerating leading-edge discriminator threshold crossing via *range walk* (detector blooming). The resulting timing distortion artificially shortens the calculated round-trip time ($t_{\text{TOF}}$), shifting the apparent obstacle boundary several centimeters toward the sensor without asserting a hardware fault.

Timing and transport anomalies can also corrupt an observation silently. If an unshielded physical interface experiences electromagnetic interference, deserializer bit slips (where the hardware drops or duplicates a bit, misaligning the entire subsequent data stream) can alter payload semantics without invalidating standard packet lengths. More dangerous than a lost packet, because nothing flags it, is an observation delivered with a timestamp that misreports its true capture epoch. If an image sensor captures photons at epoch $t_0$, but a late interrupt handler or an unsynchronized system clock timestamps the resulting memory buffer at $t_0 + \delta t$, the downstream state estimator integrates spatial features under an incorrect body pose. Consider a machine traveling with instantaneous velocity $v$ and linear acceleration $a$ along a given trajectory. When perception suffers an undetected timing desynchronization $\delta t$, the state estimator assigns the detected position of an obstacle to the body coordinates at $t_0 + \delta t$ rather than $t_0$. Over the unmodeled time interval $\delta t$, the physical state estimation error $\Delta p$ between the asserted position and the true position is governed by the kinematic drift relation (@eq-percep-kinematic-drift):
$$\Delta p = v \cdot \delta t + \frac{1}{2} a \cdot (\delta t)^2$$ {#eq-percep-kinematic-drift}

The arrival stamp of @sec-perception-handoff is a silent desynchronization of exactly this kind. At a constant drive speed the acceleration term vanishes, leaving the $v\,\tau_{\text{recv}}$ offset sized there, and nothing raises a fault flag. Because the pipeline delivers a continuous stream of valid tensors, the state estimator assumes a fresh observation, computing safe actuator trajectories from stale physics. A missing frame causes a known information loss that a state observer or policy can handle by expanding its uncertainty covariance. A frame that arrives on time with a corrupt timestamp causes the model to contract its uncertainty around an incorrect spatial state, projecting false confidence and driving actuators toward an obstacle that the model believes has already been cleared.

Defending against silent failure requires dedicated runtime health monitors at the sensor ingestion boundary. A pixel intensity histogram monitor measures the distribution of raw digitized values immediately after direct memory access transfer, identifying over-exposure saturation when values concentrate at the maximum bit depth or identifying lens occlusion when spatial variance drops below an empirical noise floor. A hardware watchdog timer tracks inter-arrival times across the direct memory access channel, flagging transport jitter when inter-frame intervals exceed $T_{\text{nominal}} + 3\sigma_{\text{jitter}}$. Higher up the stack, an optical flow plausibility monitor compares computed pixel displacement vectors against the physical velocity envelope of the body, rejecting observations that imply accelerations beyond mechanical capability. In multi-modal configurations, a cross-sensor consistency check compares high-rate (`{python} RollingShutterSkew.f_imu_str`) inertial measurement unit integrations against visual odometry. If the visual pipeline reports that the machine is stationary while the gravity-compensated inertial estimate indicates sustained $2.0\text{ m/s}^2$ linear acceleration, the monitor can flag a discrepancy once attitude, bias, timing, and measurement uncertainty are accounted for.

Every runtime health monitor sees the world only through what the transducer reported at the causal boundary of @sec-boundary-causal-boundary, so a single sensing channel cannot validate its own semantic interpretations. A camera assembly with clean optics, balanced exposure, jitter-free transport, and synchronized microsecond clocking can still present an observation that leads a learned model to hallucinate a clear path or ignore an obstacle. Because deep vision models project high-dimensional inputs through complex non-linear manifolds, in-distribution optical anomalies (such as a high-contrast shadow across an aisle, a person printed on a carton, or specular glare from shrink-wrap or a wet floor) generate plausible pixel statistics, valid optical flow fields, and high model confidence. A single-sensor monitor evaluates whether the data collection process operated within nominal limits, not whether the inferred semantics match physical reality. A second modality, such as lidar or radar, can corroborate some optical claims when its coverage and failure dependence have been checked. A separately validated permission path can enforce clearance only within its sensing, model, timing, and actuator assumptions; neither route establishes unrestricted semantic truth.

### Environmental degradation under precipitation, fog, and lens flare

Physical environments continuously degrade sensory transmission across optical, near-infrared, and radio channels. A perception architecture operating across factory yards, loading docks, or public roadways must anticipate how weather and illumination alter signal-to-noise ratios without asserting hardware error flags.

**Optical cameras in atmospheric scattering and glare**: Suspended airborne aerosol particles in fog, mist, and smoke ($1\text{--}10\,\mu\text{m}$ diameter) scatter visible wavelengths ($\lambda \approx 400\text{--}700\,\text{nm}$) under Mie scattering physics. Scene radiance attenuates exponentially across distance according to Koschmieder's law:
$$C(d) = C_0 \, e^{-\beta_{\text{atm}} d}$$
where $C_0$ is intrinsic object contrast, $d$ is metric range, and $\beta_{\text{atm}}$ is the atmospheric extinction coefficient. In moderate fog ($\beta_{\text{atm}} \approx 0.05\,\text{m}^{-1}$), apparent contrast decays below the $0.05$ perceptual detection threshold within $60\,\text{meters}$. High-frequency edge gradients dissolve into uniform background luminance, preventing convolutional and transformer backbones from forming valid feature embeddings. Airborne rain introduces high-velocity streak noise across frames, while droplets impacting the protective lens act as irregular refractive microlenses. Each droplet deflects incoming rays, creating severe localized geometric distortion, optical blur, and false object silhouettes.

**High angular velocity motion blur and MTF collapse**: During a yaw rotation or manipulator sweep, a camera center at lever arm $r$ travels a tangential distance set by angular rate $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ and exposure duration:
$$\Delta x_{\text{rot}} = r \cdot \|\boldsymbol{\omega}\| \cdot t_{\text{exp}}$$
For the illustrative wrist-mounted camera at $r = 0.5\,\text{meters}$, $\omega = 3.0\,\text{rad/s}$, and $16\,\text{ms}$ exposure, this travel scale is $\Delta x \approx 24\,\text{mm}$. It is not an image-plane blur width. Scene depth and camera projection determine the image motion due to translation, while attitude change also moves image features even without camera-center translation. Blur can attenuate the gradients used by feature matching, visual odometry, and learned perception; its effect on tracking and learned features requires evaluation over the intended motion and exposure range.

**High Dynamic Range (HDR) saturation and blooming**: In logistics, construction, and outdoor robotics, the illustrative illumination range extends from $100{,}000\,\text{lux}$ in direct sunlit outdoor yards to $300\,\text{lux}$ in shaded warehouse aisles. Standard linear CMOS sensors provide only $60\text{--}70\,\text{dB}$ of dynamic range. When a robot turns from a dim aisle toward an open sunlit loading dock, incident photon flux overwhelms the photodiode full-well charge capacity ($10{,}000\text{--}30{,}000\,e^{-}$), driving silicon photodiodes into deep saturation. Excess photo-generated electrons overflow past barrier implants into adjacent pixel wells (**charge blooming**), wiping out entire array regions into uniform saturated white ($255$). Internal reflections between lens elements create veiling glare and flare streaks, eliminating the spatial contrast required for disparity matching and optical flow.

**LiDAR in airborne particulates, retroreflector blooming, and specular surfaces**: Pulsed time-of-flight LiDAR ($905\,\text{nm}$ and $1{,}550\,\text{nm}$) suffers three distinct physical failure mechanisms in industrial and outdoor operation:

1. *Aerosol backscatter clutter*: Emitted laser pulses strike suspended fog droplets and dust particulates, scattering optical power directly back into the receiver during the initial nanoseconds of flight. This generates dense near-field point clutter—often appearing as a solid "phantom wall" within $0.5\text{--}3.0\,\text{meters}$ of the aperture. Downstream spatial clustering algorithms interpret these returns as immediate collision obstacles, triggering false emergency stops. Concurrently, forward beam attenuation depletes pulse energy, truncating effective range by over 70 percent in heavy rain or dense fog.
2. *Retroreflector detector blooming and range walk*: High-visibility safety vests, barcode placards, and vehicle license plates incorporate retroreflective prismatic surfaces designed to return incoming light directly along the emission axis with gain factors $10^3\text{--}10^4$ higher than diffuse surfaces. When this overwhelming optical pulse strikes the APD or SPAD receiver, the pre-amplifier saturates. Non-linear leading-edge discriminator crossing accelerates pulse triggering, introducing a **range walk** error that artificially shortens the calculated flight time by several centimeters, while trailing charge dissipation blurs the retroreflector into a long radial streak of phantom points.
3. *Specular surfaces and non-Lambertian forward bounce*: Triangulation sensors, structured light, and LiDAR rely on the physical assumption of diffuse Lambertian scattering. Specular surfaces—including polished warehouse concrete floors, shrink-wrapped palletized freight, metallic shelving, and architectural glass—violate this assumption. Emitted laser pulses undergo specular forward reflection ($r_{\text{reflected}} = r_{\text{incident}}$), directing light away from the sensor. On wet floors, this creates artificial zero-return dropouts ("puddle black holes"); on glass walls or metal panels, it induces multi-bounce reflections, projecting phantom obstacle points meters behind walls or beneath the floor.

**FMCW radar all-weather resilience**: Operating at $76\text{--}81\,\text{GHz}$, FMCW millimeter-wave radar features a wavelength of $\lambda \approx 3.9\,\text{mm}$—roughly 4,000 times larger than optical laser pulses and substantially larger than fog aerosol droplets ($1\text{--}10\,\mu\text{m}$). Scattering by airborne particles follows Rayleigh scattering physics, where the particle scattering cross-section $\sigma_s$ scales inversely with the fourth power of wavelength:
$$\sigma_s \propto \frac{d_{\text{droplet}}^6}{\lambda^4}$$
This wavelength dependence explains radar's reduced sensitivity to small airborne particles in the Rayleigh regime; it does not establish immunity to weather. Ground reflections can create multipath ghost targets, and water films on a radome can attenuate the signal. A sensor suite must therefore qualify the remaining radar coverage when optical observations degrade.

### Out-of-distribution detection and epistemic uncertainty

A structurally valid observation tensor produced by an unoccluded, calibrated sensor can still cause downstream machine learning models to hallucinate dangerous outputs. In physical AI, uncertainty decomposes into two distinct types: **aleatoric uncertainty**\index{Uncertainty!aleatoric} (irreducible stochastic variance arising from physical sensor transduction, such as photon shot noise or aerosol scattering) and **epistemic uncertainty**\index{Uncertainty!epistemic} (model ignorance arising from unrepresented scene geometry, novel objects, or covariate shifts outside the training distribution). Deep vision backbones and vision-language-action policies project high-dimensional inputs onto lower-dimensional learned manifolds. When exposed to out-of-distribution (OOD) scenes—such as overturned cargo pallets, novel emergency strobe patterns, reflective high-visibility vests, or industrial smoke plumes—deep networks fail silently. Standard softmax normalization enforces $\sum_k p_k = 1$ over the modeled classes; it provides no separate guarantee that the input belongs to one of them.

Runtime OOD monitors test whether an input departs from the conditions used to qualify the model. Their scores can trigger refusal, but a score inside the accepted range does not establish that the scene was interpreted correctly. Candidate mechanisms operating at the inference boundary include:

1. **Feature-space energy and Mahalanobis scoring**: Softmax probabilities are notoriously uncalibrated for anomaly detection. Instead, runtime monitors evaluate the Helmholtz free energy score across the unnormalized logits $f(\mathbf{x})$ of the vision backbone (@eq-percep-free-energy):
$$E(\mathbf{x}; f) = -T \cdot \log \sum_{k=1}^K \exp\left(\frac{f_k(\mathbf{x})}{T}\right)$$ {#eq-percep-free-energy}
Here $T>0$ is a score-temperature parameter, not a physical sensor temperature; its choice and the decision threshold require calibration. An energy threshold is useful only to the extent that validation separates the intended inputs from relevant anomalies. In metric embedding layers, class-conditional Gaussian models evaluate the squared Mahalanobis distance against the training distribution centroids $\boldsymbol{\mu}_c$ and pooled covariance $\mathbf{\Sigma}$ (@eq-percep-ood-mahalanobis):
$$d_M^2(\mathbf{z}) = \min_c (\mathbf{z} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_c)^\top \mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{z} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_c)$$ {#eq-percep-ood-mahalanobis}
flagging feature vectors that fall outside empirical confidence ellipsoids.

2. **Epistemic uncertainty quantification**: While offline architectures can sample Monte Carlo dropout across successive forward passes, real-time physical loops cannot afford the resulting latency multiplier ($N \times t_{\text{infer}}$). Production systems instead deploy single-pass estimators—such as multi-head deep ensembles sharing a common trunk or evidential deep learning heads predicting Dirichlet parameter distributions $\text{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})$—to extract prediction variance in a single forward pass. The total evidential strength $S = \sum_{k=1}^K \alpha_k$ directly yields the epistemic vacuity $u$ (@eq-percep-evidential-vacuity):
$$u = \frac{K}{S} = \frac{K}{\sum_{k=1}^K \alpha_k}$$ {#eq-percep-evidential-vacuity}
as a model-dependent uncertainty score. Its interpretation and fault-detection coverage still require empirical qualification.

3. **Generative feature reconstruction**: Ingested feature maps are routed through a lightweight bottleneck autoencoder trained exclusively on nominal operational data. Novel geometry or degraded inputs may produce high latent reconstruction residuals $\|\mathbf{z} - \hat{\mathbf{z}}\|^2$ that a calibrated threshold can flag; some anomalies can still reconstruct well.

When an OOD monitor trips, the perception engine sets the `BIT_OOD_DETECTED` flag in the observation record's health bitmask.
