The permission path uses this flag to refuse high-speed autonomous motions, expand clearance safety buffers, or invoke deterministic supervisory takeovers. In multi-sensor configurations, this bitmask triggers cross-modal arbitration: if the optical camera sets `BIT_OPTICAL_SATURATED` or `BIT_OOD_DETECTED` while the FMCW radar maintains valid Doppler returns, the fusion pipeline demotes optical tokens and elevates radar range claims, provided the remaining modality can support the required clearance claim within its own validated conditions.

::: {#ws-perception-tesla-williston-omission .callout-war-story title="Silent perception omission (2016)"}
**Context**: A 2015 Tesla Model S\index{Incidents!Williston accident} traveling at about $74\text{ mph}$ with Traffic-Aware Cruise Control and Autosteer active struck a refrigerated semitrailer turning left across its path near Williston, Florida [@ntsb2017tesla].

**Mechanism**: The crossing-path collision lay outside the front-to-rear crash modes for which the 2015 warning and automatic braking systems were designed. NHTSA reported that automatic braking required agreement between camera and radar; unusual vehicle shapes could impede camera classification ([NHTSA ODI PE16-007](https://static.nhtsa.gov/odi/inv/2016/INCLA-PE16007-7876.PDF)).

**Impact**: The NTSB found no recorded indication that forward collision warning or automatic emergency braking detected an object, and no pre-impact braking occurred. The car passed under the trailer, which sheared off its roof (@fig-08-real-ntsb-williston-crash).

**Response**: The NTSB examined operational design domain limits and driver engagement as well as the collision-avoidance systems.

**Systems lesson**: An absent detection is not evidence that a crossing path is clear. A permission design must account for detection coverage and unsupported scenarios; a health flag cannot certify that every relevant object was perceived.
:::

::: {#fig-08-real-ntsb-williston-crash fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Williston collision damage**: This NTSB presentation slide shows damage on the right side of the semitrailer and the roofless Tesla after the 2016 crash. The crossing-path geometry and absence of pre-impact braking come from the [NTSB accident report](https://www.ntsb.gov/investigations/AccidentReports/Reports/HAR1702.pdf), not from the photographs alone. Photographs credited on the NTSB slide to Florida Highway Patrol." fig-alt="NTSB slide with two photographs: left, a refrigerated semitrailer with damage low on its right side; right, a heavily damaged roofless Tesla. Yellow ovals mark damage areas. The photos do not show the vehicles' motion or collision angle."}
![](images/png/fig08_real_ntsb_williston_crash.png){width="90%"}
:::

Whatever record the producer attaches to an observation can expose only the faults the producer can check. The detectable faults and the timing and calibration conditions fit in such a record; silent semantic errors, like the omission at Williston, still require separate evidence.

## The Observation Contract {#sec-perception-observation-contract}

A downstream tracker, policy backbone, or the permission path cannot reconstruct exposure timing, mounting calibration, or record integrity from a raw tensor alone. The perception producer therefore wraps each observation in a formal contract record—the **Perception Evidence** record (the seventh contract in the machine stack's 14-record contract lineage)—and the observation is unusable without a capture epoch, a clock identifier, a bounded conversion to the permission path's clock, and a calibration inside its validity range, whose revision the frame identifier carries; the consumer refuses a record that lacks any of them before reading the payload. The clock domain and the $\mathcal{H}_1$ age budget come from the handoff record of @sec-nervous-handoffs-matrix, which this record consumes, and perception supplies the capture-side fields that let a consumer check an observation against them.

An observation tokenizer can expose the same record to a VLA policy or neural state estimator. The modality determines the payload: image features, metric returns, motion events, or contact deformation. The common interface preserves when and where that payload was measured and what uncertainty accompanies it.

Across all modalities, the observation tokenizer binds the sensory payload token $\mathbf{z}_{\text{sensor}}$ with continuous temporal positional embeddings ($\mathbf{e}_{\Delta t} = \text{Fourier}(t_{\text{current}} - t_0)$), coordinate frame prefix embeddings ($\mathbf{e}_{\text{frame}} = \text{MLP}(\mathbf{T}_{bc})$), and spatial covariance tokens ($\mathbf{e}_{\Sigma} = \text{MLP}(\text{vec}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_z))$) (@eq-percep-vla-obs-tokenizer):
$$\mathbf{z}_{\text{token}} = [\mathbf{z}_{\text{sensor}}, \mathbf{e}_{\Delta t}, \mathbf{e}_{\text{frame}}, \mathbf{e}_{\Sigma}]$$ {#eq-percep-vla-obs-tokenizer}
This representation makes time, frame, and uncertainty available to the learned model. Qualification still depends on the clock, calibration, residual, and health checks; encoding their values as tokens cannot replace those checks.

::: {#dfn-perception-observation-contract .callout-definition title="Perception evidence (observation contract)"}

***Perception Evidence record***\index{Perception Evidence!definition}\index{Observation contract!definition}\index{Perception!observation contract} (the observation contract, the seventh contract in the machine stack's lineage) is the formal cyber-physical specification governing sensory data structures traversing computational boundaries, binding a raw observation tensor or extracted geometric bounding envelope to its exposure midpoint timestamp ($t_{\text{capture}}$), capture clock identifier, synchronization error bound ($\epsilon_{\text{sync}}$), sensor coordinate frame identifier, positive-semidefinite spatial covariance matrix ($\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$), qualified clearance inset ($C_{\text{inset}}$), and hardware health bitmask (@eq-percep-observation-contract-tuple):
$$\mathcal{O} = \langle t_{\text{capture}}, \text{clock\_id}, \epsilon_{\text{sync}}, \text{frame\_id}, \mathbf{T}_{\text{payload}}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, C_{\text{inset}}, \text{mask}_{\text{health}}, \text{crc32} \rangle$$ {#eq-percep-observation-contract-tuple}

1.  **Significance**: Emits dated spatial claims, bounding envelopes ($C_{\text{inset}}$), and covariance matrices ($\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$) to Scene Memory (@sec-memory, which consumes this contract to emit Contract 8, the Scene Memory State record) and Trajectory Planning (@sec-planning), allowing downstream observers, policy backbones, and the permission path to compute upper information age, select valid coordinate transforms, and bound spatial error before any claim influences a motion proposal.
2.  **Distinction**: An observation contract is not an alternative to serialization formats like Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers, or ROS 2 IDL; it can be serialized using any of them. The distinction lies in semantic invariants: while a transport schema guarantees only data type layout (e.g., float arrays and strings), an observation contract enforces cyber-physical invariants—binding monotonic capture epochs ($t_0$), hardware clock synchronization bounds ($\epsilon_{\text{sync}}$), validated coordinate frame transformations, and bounded spatial error quantiles before any payload data is admitted to the control loop.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating perception output as a pure geometric coordinate $[x, y, z]^\top$ without propagating its spatial covariance or sensor health bitmask, blinding downstream safety filters to sensor occlusion or degraded lighting.

:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-nav-observation-record
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NAVIGATION-CAMERA OBSERVATION RECORD, FILLED
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The filled column of @tbl-08-observation-record-schema and the
# │          clock-conversion paragraph that follows it.
# │
# │ Goal:    Fill the observation record for the mobile manipulator's
# │          navigation camera and size the consumer's upper age at dispatch.
# │ Show:    age at dispatch 51.6 ms; clock-conversion bound 0.2 ms; upper
# │          age 51.8 ms, equal to the refusal threshold (budgeted age plus
# │          bound); frame counter at 60 Hz; the bound's 0.3 mm of travel at
# │          the 1.5 m/s drive limit, carried inside delta_loc rather than
# │          charged as a budget row.
# │ How:     AISLE.perception_age (the latency waterfall above); eps_sync is a
# │          chapter LOAD value that the spatial-belief record of @sec-memory
# │          reuses; RM.nav_camera frame rate; displacement via
# │          calc_spatial_information_age_displacement.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, fmt_length, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class NavObservationRecord:
    """Filled observation record for the running machine's navigation camera."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    camera = RM.nav_camera  # category: datasheet (registry: Sony IMX477 navigation camera)
    f_frame = camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond)  # category: derived
    eps_sync = 0.2 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (capture-to-MCU clock-conversion bound; reused by @sec-memory)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity.to(meter / second)  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    upper_age = (t_age + eps_sync).to(millisecond)
    refuse_threshold = (AISLE.perception_age + eps_sync).to(millisecond)  # refusal threshold: budgeted age plus the conversion bound
    dx_sync = calc_spatial_information_age_displacement(v, eps_sync).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_age.magnitude - 51.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected age at dispatch: {t_age}")
    check(abs(eps_sync.to(millisecond).magnitude - 0.2) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected clock-conversion bound: {eps_sync}")
    check(abs(upper_age.magnitude - 51.8) < 0.05, f"Unexpected upper age at dispatch: {upper_age}")
    check(abs(refuse_threshold.magnitude - 51.8) < 0.05, f"Unexpected refusal threshold: {refuse_threshold}")
    check(abs((refuse_threshold - upper_age).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Prose says the dispatched upper age meets the refusal threshold exactly")
    check(abs(f_frame.to(ureg.hertz).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected navigation-camera frame rate: {f_frame}")
    check(abs(dx_sync.magnitude - 0.3) < 0.005, f"Unexpected travel during the clock-conversion bound: {dx_sync}")
    check(dx_sync < delta_loc, "Prose says the clock-conversion travel fits inside delta_loc")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    eps_sync_str = fmt_latency(eps_sync.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    upper_age_str = fmt_latency(upper_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    refuse_threshold_str = fmt_latency(refuse_threshold, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    f_frame_str = fmt_frequency(f_frame, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    dx_sync_str = fmt_length(dx_sync, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
```

| Record field                               | Meaning                                                           | Consumer check                                                                                     | Navigation camera                                                                                                           |
|:-------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `capture_timestamp_ns`, `capture_clock_id` | Exposure midpoint in one shared, monotonic capture clock          | Convert to safety microcontroller (MCU) time with a valid bounded-skew mapping before checking age | Exposure midpoint on clock `cam_nav`; dispatched `{python} NavObservationRecord.t_age_str` later (@tbl-08-latency-budget)   |
| `sync_error_ns`                            | Bound on capture-to-MCU clock conversion error                    | Add to worst-case age; refuse if missing or expired                                                | `{python} NavObservationRecord.eps_sync_str`, so the upper age at dispatch is `{python} NavObservationRecord.upper_age_str` |
| `sequence_index`                           | Monotonic camera frame counter                                    | Detect gaps and reordering                                                                         | One count per frame at `{python} NavObservationRecord.f_frame_str`                                                          |
| `sensor_frame_id`                          | Transform-tree key and calibration revision                       | Select the valid extrinsic transform                                                               | `nav_cam` with its calibration revision                                                                                     |
| `tensor_payload`                           | Format, dimensions, length, and buffer                            | Validate bounds and record checksum before reading                                                 | Raw/debayered image tensor or point-cloud buffer                                                                            |
| `bounding_envelope`                        | Bounding volume $[dx, dy, dz]$ or qualified clearance inset       | Bound occupied volume and inflate safety sets ($C_{\text{inset}}$)                                 | Metric corridor bounds inflated by validated quantile                                                                       |
| `spatial_covariance`                       | Positive-semidefinite spatial error scale                         | Use with separately calibrated bias and tail bounds                                                | Point-wise or object-centric covariance matrix $\mathbf{\Sigma}_z$                                                          |
| `calibration_metadata`                     | Intrinsics, extrinsics, coefficients, temperature, validity range | Reject calibration outside its validated region                                                    | Factory pinhole $\mathbf{K}$ and chassis extrinsic transform $\mathbf{T}_{bc}$                                              |
| `provenance_digest`                        | SHA-256 of firmware and model revisions                           | Match the approved build; this is not payload integrity                                            | Signed hash of vision backbone weights and firmware                                                                         |
| `payload_crc32`                            | CRC over serialized header (excluding this field) and payload     | Detect accidental record corruption; not authentication                                            | 32-bit cyclical redundancy check                                                                                            |
| `health_bitmask`                           | Hardware, degradation, and perception validity flags              | Refuse claims with safety-critical faults or OOD flags                                             | Sync-loss, link, saturation, rain/fog clutter, and OOD bits; input-support bits from @sec-evaluation-limits                 |

: **Perception Evidence record schema (observation contract)**: Compact fields needed to date and frame a claim, evaluate its uncertainty, bounding envelope, and health flags, and check the bytes and generating revision. The last column fills the fields this chapter computes for the mobile manipulator's navigation camera; its dispatch age and clock-conversion bound are illustrative. A keyed authenticator is a separate requirement if the threat model includes malicious modification. {#tbl-08-observation-record-schema tbl-colwidths="[23,23,26,28]"}

The fields in @tbl-08-observation-record-schema date each observation and its generating revision. The capture timestamp is monotonic, not nanoseconds since the UNIX epoch. A rolling-shutter claim must identify the row or region whose acquisition time it represents, and `sequence_index` detects missing frames independently of clock conversion. If the MCU has a different clock, a synchronization service supplies a versioned conversion $t_{\text{MCU}}=a t_{\text{capture}}+b$, its validity interval, and the measured error bound $\epsilon_{\text{sync}}$.

At dispatch, the producer records the upper age $t_{\text{MCU,dispatch}}-t_{\text{MCU,capture}}+\epsilon_{\text{sync}}$. That value describes a past checkpoint. At admission, the evidence is older by $\Delta_{\text{da}}$; at later consumption it is older still. The permission path must use its current monotonic time and the original capture epoch, rather than replaying the dispatch-age value as if physical time had stopped. A new proposal based on the same observation does not refresh its evidence.

For the navigation camera, the **dispatch-local** threshold is `{python} NavObservationRecord.t_age_str` plus the `{python} NavObservationRecord.eps_sync_str` conversion bound, or `{python} NavObservationRecord.refuse_threshold_str`. The illustrative frame reaches that threshold exactly at dispatch, leaving no extra dispatch-stage allowance for batching or host contention. The budget charges the `{python} NavObservationRecord.t_age_str` pipeline interval as distance; the clock bound's `{python} NavObservationRecord.dx_sync_str` travel is carried inside $\delta_{\text{loc}}$. Neither convention removes post-dispatch physical aging.

Admission requires a separately qualified current-age limit that includes the dispatch-to-admission bound and leaves room for the active lease and physical response. The present partial ledger has not established that limit, so the filled record demonstrates qualified field construction, not an admitted full-speed trajectory. Once $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ is bounded, the engineer can close the stopping calculation or reduce speed to recover margin. Each elapsed interval appears once: if a budget starts at admission, it includes the prior evidence age plus the subsequent lease; if it starts at capture, it accounts for the same timeline without adding those intervals again.

The transform key and calibration revision anchor metric coordinates.[^fn-hw-thermal-drift] The firmware/model digest supports version provenance; `payload_crc32` detects accidental changes to the actual header and payload after serialization. Neither a checksum nor a build hash proves semantic truth, and neither authenticates an adversarial producer without a keyed check.

[^fn-hw-thermal-drift]: **Mechanical thermal expansion**\index{Hardware!thermal expansion}: For a stereo baseline $b =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.b_str` and an unmodeled change $|\delta b| =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.db_str`, first-order geometry gives $|\delta z|/z\approx|\delta b|/b$. At $z =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.z_thermal_str`, the corresponding depth bias is about `{python} StereoDepthError.dz_thermal_str`, assuming focal length and disparity are otherwise unchanged. Temperature compensation must be checked against the actual mount and calibration.

In the health bitmask, the lower bits report hardware faults such as synchronization loss or transport errors; intermediate bits report environmental degradation (such as lens saturation or aerosol backscatter); and the upper bits report perceptual validity concerns such as occlusion or out-of-distribution inputs outside the support the evaluation tested. These input-support bits implement the runtime monitor specified in @sec-evaluation-limits. A set safety-critical bit requires refusal of the affected claim.

The explicit record layout also supports fault injection. A test can alter the capture time, omit a sequence number, inflate reported covariance, or set an occlusion flag, then check whether the consumer rejects or degrades that claim within its budget. Such mutations verify response to the injected record faults; physical glare, miscalibration, and actuator behavior still require separate tests in @sec-verification.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Observation contract mutations feed the hardware-in-the-loop verification harness in @sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection.
:::

::: {#chk-percep-observation-contract-triage .callout-checkpoint title="Observation record checks"}

Before passing raw sensor observations into downstream policy backbones and state observers, verify your understanding of observation record contracts:

- [ ] **Record triage**: Can you explain why a health bit, checksum, valid clock conversion, and freshness check must precede consumption of a spatial claim?
- [ ] **Timestamp corruption vs. dropped packets**: Can you describe why receiving a sensory frame with a desynchronized timestamp degrades spatial state estimation and policy grounding far more severely than dropping the packet entirely?
- [ ] **Deterministic fault injection**: Can you distinguish between physically perturbing optical sensors vs. deterministically mutating fields in the shared-memory observation record during automated hardware-in-the-loop verification?
:::

### Applying a delayed observation {#sec-perception-discrete-state-estimation}

A correct capture epoch makes delayed measurements usable when the consumer has a qualified history and motion model. This implementation detail supports the contract; maintaining state through subsequent occlusion and deciding its expiry belong to @sec-memory. Here $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ denotes the estimated state, $\mathbf{P}$ its covariance, $\mathbf{H}$ the measurement model, and $\mathbf{K}$ the correction gain. The Kalman update combines a prediction with a measurement using their uncertainty; @sec-appendix-control-covariance develops the covariance dynamics, and @sec-appendix-control-lqr develops the estimation/control relationship.

A delayed visual observation must correct the state at its capture epoch before the estimator propagates the correction to the present. One implementation retains historical states and inertial inputs in an **out-of-sequence ring buffer** with $N_{\text{buffer}} = \lceil T_{\text{buffer}} / \Delta t_{\text{IMU}} \rceil$ slots. Its horizon $T_{\text{buffer}}$ bounds the delay it can accommodate. When observation $\mathbf{z}_{t_0}$ arrives at $t_{\text{recv}}$, the estimator retrieves the prediction at $t_0$, computes its innovation and gain, and applies the historical correction (@eq-percep-oosm-correction):
$$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_0|t_0} = \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_0|t_0-1} + \mathbf{K}_{t_0} (\mathbf{z}_{t_0} - \mathbf{H}_{t_0} \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_0|t_0-1}), \quad \mathbf{P}_{t_0|t_0} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_{t_0}\mathbf{H}_{t_0}) \mathbf{P}_{t_0|t_0-1}$$ {#eq-percep-oosm-correction}
For the following propagation-only replay, assume no intervening measurement updates. If other sensors corrected the state during the interval, their updates must also be replayed in timestamp order. The estimator then executes a fast replay pass—re-integrating buffered IMU samples from $t_0$ to $t_{\text{recv}}$ using the updated initial condition $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_0|t_0}$—to bring the current state estimate $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{\text{recv}}}$ into alignment with the new observation without introducing non-causal state discontinuities (@eq-percep-oosm-replay):
$$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{\text{recv}}} = \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_0|t_0} + \sum_{\tau = t_0}^{t_{\text{recv}}-1} \mathbf{f}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_\tau, \mathbf{u}_\tau) \Delta t_{\text{IMU}}$$ {#eq-percep-oosm-replay}
with covariance forward replay governed by state transition matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}(t_{\text{recv}}, t_0) = \prod_{\tau = t_0}^{t_{\text{recv}}-1} \mathbf{F}_\tau$:
$$\mathbf{P}_{t_{\text{recv}}} = \mathbf{\Phi}(t_{\text{recv}}, t_0) \mathbf{P}_{t_0|t_0} \mathbf{\Phi}^\top(t_{\text{recv}}, t_0) + \sum_{\tau = t_0}^{t_{\text{recv}}-1} \mathbf{\Phi}(t_{\text{recv}}, \tau+1) \mathbf{Q}_\tau \mathbf{\Phi}^\top(t_{\text{recv}}, \tau+1)$$ {#eq-percep-oosm-cov-replay}
This rewind-and-replay routine (@eq-percep-oosm-cov-replay) is strictly bounded by ring buffer horizon $T_{\text{buffer}}$. If pipeline jitter or memory bus contention stretches observation age such that $t_{\text{age}} > T_{\text{buffer}}$, the ring buffer has already overwritten epoch $t_0$. The estimator must refuse the delayed measurement, allow process noise $\mathbf{Q}$ to inflate the predictive covariance $\mathbf{P}$, and alert the downstream permission path that visual grounding has lapsed.

**Observation tokens in end-to-end VLA policies**: In vision-language-action (VLA) architectures, policy backbones face the identical out-of-sequence dilemma. An image captured at $t_0$ produces visual patch tokens that reach the transformer attention blocks after forward-pass and transport latency $t_{\text{age}}$. A policy $\mathbf{a}_t = \pi(\mathbf{z}_{t_0})$ that receives neither elapsed time nor current state cannot distinguish otherwise identical images with different downstream delays. A VLA can expose the same timing and state information by formatting inputs as composite, typed observation tokens (@eq-percep-vla-token-embedding):
$$\mathbf{z}_{\text{obs}} = \mathbf{W}_v \mathbf{z}_{\text{patch}} + \mathbf{W}_t \mathbf{e}_{\Delta t} + \mathbf{W}_s \mathbf{e}_{\text{state}} + \mathbf{e}_{\text{frame}}$$ {#eq-percep-vla-token-embedding}
where projected visual patch embeddings $\mathbf{z}_{\text{patch}}$ are added to a continuous temporal token embedding $\mathbf{e}_{\Delta t} = \text{Fourier}(t_{\text{current}} - t_0)$, a forward-propagated kinematic state token $\mathbf{e}_{\text{state}} = \text{MLP}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{\text{current}}})$, and a calibrated reference frame embedding $\mathbf{e}_{\text{frame}}$. These inputs let the policy condition its proposal on elapsed time and the estimated execution state; training and evaluation must establish whether it uses them effectively. The token representation supplies timing and state information to the learned policy; it does not validate the estimate or grant the resulting action permission.

A delayed update can improve the state estimate while preserving the original evidence epoch. Neither that update nor a passed record check proves that the observation is semantically correct; the following mistakes confuse qualified representation with physical truth.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-perception-fallacies-pitfalls}

Perception\index{Perception} must describe the world within the strict temporal deadlines required for control actuation. Semantic confidence and high spatial accuracy cannot compensate for pipelines that deliver stale observations, fuse asynchronous exposures, or read average bandwidth as a bound on one frame's age.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Accepting an observation because its semantic classification confidence is high, regardless of its age.*

The mobile manipulator receives a high-confidence observation that the rack end ahead is clear, but a stall in the vision pipeline\index{Perception!pipeline latency} delivers it several frames late. A person who stepped out after the exposure is absent from that frame. The confidence score\index{Confidence score} describes the earlier image, not present clearance. Accepting the packet as current can therefore authorize motion toward an occupied rack end. The perception interface must check measurement age against its refusal threshold (@sec-perception-observation-contract)\index{Observation!freshness limit} and reject observations that exceed it. Any continued state propagation\index{State estimation!propagation} without new data must carry kinematic uncertainty covariances\index{Kinematics!uncertainty} together with qualified residual tails or hard bounds on dynamic-obstacle reachability, allowing the controller to enforce safety envelopes\index{Safety!envelope} as historical evidence ages. *A softmax score certifies neither distribution membership, temporal freshness, nor physical clearance.*

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Fusing multi-sensor observations without a clock bound derived from the tolerated spatial error.*

Two cameras on the mobile manipulator watch the same rack upright while the base drives at its `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.v_str` drive limit, but their clocks differ by $\Delta t_{\text{skew}}$. Treating the two exposure times\index{Exposure time} as equal places the upright $v\,\Delta t_{\text{skew}}$ apart in the two views, and track association\index{Track association} can then split one physical object into two conflicting tracks ("ghosting"). Spatial calibration\index{Calibration!spatial} cannot correct an unknown temporal offset. The synchronization requirement must follow the tolerated position error and maximum relevant speed, expressed by $\Delta t_{\text{skew}} \le \epsilon_{\text{pos}} / v_{\text{max}}$. Hardware synchronization\index{Hardware!clock synchronization} at exposure time makes that bound enforceable; selecting a timing technology (like Precision Time Protocol, IEEE 1588 PTP\index{IEEE 1588 PTP}) without first checking the spatial error budget leaves the fusion assumption unverified.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Inferring a critical read's deadline from average camera bandwidth.*

An acceptable average utilization says nothing about how long one read waits behind a synchronized capture and inference burst. On the mobile manipulator no permission-path read waits behind the burst, because the microcontroller reads from its own memory; the burst instead ages the frame or delays the chunk that the application processor is preparing (@sec-perception-cost-ingestion), so the quantities to verify under the synchronized burst are the host's capture-to-dispatch age and its renewal interval, not its average bandwidth.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Assuming an end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy implicitly learns to compensate for rolling shutter and sensor latency without explicit temporal tokenization.*

A common assumption in deep imitation learning is that large vision-language-action policies trained on extensive robot teleoperation datasets will automatically learn to predict actions that compensate for image distortion and communication latency. In practice, demonstration datasets are collected under varying chassis velocities, camera modes, and host bus loads. Because the model receives only raw pixels without capture timestamps or row readout indices, the network cannot disambiguate physical obstacle geometry from rolling-shutter scanline shearing or latency-induced travel. Such ambiguity can compound closed-loop errors. The familiar $O(T^2 \epsilon)$ behavior-cloning bound concerns accumulated cost under its assumptions, with horizon $T$ and imitation error $\epsilon$; it is not a universal spatial-error or oscillation law. Capture time deltas ($\Delta t = t_{\text{current}} - t_0$) and propagated kinematic state can expose the missing information. Explicit tokenization is one implementation; evaluation must establish its effectiveness, and independent permission checks remain necessary.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Treating neural depth network outputs as calibrated geometric covariances without empirical residual validation.*

Monocular depth estimation backbones and BEV lifting transformers output continuous depth maps or discrete depth-bin categorical distributions. Engineers often mistake these softmax distributions or network confidence heads for calibrated geometric uncertainties ($\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$), passing them directly to Kalman filters or safety barrier functions. However, neural depth scores are uncalibrated model confidences that correlate poorly with true physical error tails. On novel textures, specular reflections, or edge silhouettes, depth networks produce gross multimodal outliers that lie dozens of standard deviations from ground truth. Downstream clearance insets ($C_{\text{inset}}$) must never rely on raw neural variance; they require empirical validation against heavy-tailed residual distributions and hard bounds verified by active ranging sensors (LiDAR or radar).

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Relying exclusively on line-of-sight optical sensing for manipulation without tactile contact feedback.*

During some reaches and grasps, the robot's end-effector structures (fingers, palm, and wrist) occlude the contact region. Optical cameras cannot observe contact normal forces, shear stress distributions, or incipient micro-slip at the physical boundary. Assuming that high-resolution visual perception alone can guarantee grasp stability leads to dropped fragile objects or excessive motor torques that crush delicate structures. A task that depends on detecting slip or contact forces at that occluded patch needs suitable contact evidence. Tactile sensing such as elastomeric shear tracking can supply it; other tasks may instead rely on qualified force sensing, constrained fixtures, or passive grasp mechanics. The required feedback follows the contact decision, not a universal sensor prescription.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Assuming active LiDAR and depth sensors are immune to specular reflections and multipath interference in built environments.*

Engineers frequently assume that because LiDAR and active depth sensors emit their own structured energy, they are impervious to optical lighting pitfalls. In physical industrial settings with polished concrete floors, metallic shelving, architectural glass, and shrink-wrapped freight, active beams violate the diffuse Lambertian scattering assumption. Emitted pulses undergo specular forward reflection, producing artificial zero-return dropouts ("puddle black holes") on wet or polished floors, while multi-bounce reflections generate phantom obstacles located meters behind walls or beneath the floor plane. The observation pipeline must validate return intensity distributions and cross-corroborate surface geometry against inertial and radar channels.

:::

## Summary {#sec-perception-summary}

A perception result is usable only when its capture time, clock conversion, coordinate frame, and error qualification fit the proposed motion. The navigation camera's capture-to-dispatch age contributes a concrete stopping-budget term, but evidence continues aging through proposal computation, transport, and admission. The filled dispatch record does not close that later interval. A measured dispatch-to-admission bound must join the ledger before the current-age limit and active lease can support the integrated stopping claim. Dating a frame by arrival or freezing its age at dispatch hides elapsed time; neither restores physical clearance.

Spatial error is spent from the same clearance. Stereo depth error grows with squared range under fixed disparity noise, an extrinsic shift adds a lever-arm error that grows with distance, and neither a covariance nor a learned depth score supplies a 99th-percentile clearance bound by itself. A clearance inset rests on validated residuals, checked bias, and a stated tail risk or hard bound.

The failures that matter most are the silent ones, from a misdated frame to a saturated image or a hallucinated clear path, because none of them raises a fault flag. The observation contract lets the consumer refuse whatever it can check before reading the payload (capture epoch, clock conversion, frame, calibration, integrity, and health), and semantic truth still requires independent evidence.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Spatial perception and age of information"}
* **Observation Age Begins at Capture:**\index{Perception!observation age} Hardware-latched exposure time, row timing when relevant, and bounded clock conversion let the consumer compute an upper age before admitting motion.
* **Latency Converts to Blind Distance:**\index{Perception!blind distance} Total latency from photon integration to motor torque rise translates into unobserved physical displacement ($d_{\text{blind}} = v \cdot \tau_{\text{delay}}$), directly consuming physical clearance margins.
* **Choose the Measurement for the Decision:**\index{Perception!multimodal fusion} Appearance, metric range, radial velocity, changing edges, and contact deformation answer different physical questions. Complementary sensors help only when their coverage and correlated failure modes have been qualified.
* **Occupancy Precedes Identity Confirmation:**\index{Spatial representation!agency} A tentative identity does not hide a fresh occupied-region claim. Decisions that require confirmed identity or velocity must charge confirmation delay; track termination does not establish free space.
* **Rolling-Shutter Distortion Warps Learned Features:**\index{Hardware!rolling shutter} Progressive scanline readout shears straight physical edges under motion ($\Delta x = v \cdot y \cdot t_{\text{row}}$), corrupting vision transformer patch tokens and inducing false depth gradients in neural networks unless de-skewed with high-rate IMU data.
* **A Wrong Timestamp Is Worse Than a Lost Frame:**\index{Perception!timestamp integrity} A dropped frame widens spatial uncertainty; a plausible but misdated frame contracts uncertainty around the wrong pose. Clock bounds, sequence counters, and age checks must precede any use of the payload.
* **A Model Score Is Not Geometric Uncertainty:**\index{Machine Learning!geometric uncertainty} A classification or depth-bin score does not supply a calibrated spatial tail. Metric covariance, bias, and residual validation are separate inputs to a clearance decision.
* **Typed Observation Contracts Ground VLA Policies:**\index{Perception!observation contract} Typed observation tokens expose capture epochs, coordinate frames, and uncertainty to a learned policy. Their presence does not prove that the policy compensates for delay or that its proposed motion is admissible.
* **Calibration Can Change:**\index{Perception!calibration drift} Shock or temperature can alter the sensor-to-body extrinsic transform. The chapter's `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.theta_ext_str` rad extrinsic shift at `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.z_ext_str` projects to `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.dx_ext_str` laterally, as large as the whole $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ allowance. A shift of that size invalidates the calibration and requires refusal of affected claims, so every calibration carries a validity interval that the consumer checks.
* **Health Flags Cannot Certify Semantics:**\index{Perception!silent failure} A structurally valid record from a healthy sensor can still describe a clear path that is not there. A second modality narrows that gap only when its coverage and failure dependence have been checked.
* **Perception Provides Dated Snapshots:**\index{Perception!dated snapshots} Persistent spatial memory propagates state and uncertainty between observations and through occlusion; the permission path still checks whether that propagated claim fits the motion margin.
:::

Perception makes useful action possible by locating obstacles, identifying candidate contacts, and estimating motion from complementary measurements. Its output is evidence tied to a capture time and geometric frame. Once a person passes behind the rack, the machine must preserve what that evidence supports while accounting for what could have changed out of view.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From sensory photons to spatial memory"}
Perception delivers dated observations, but the person at the rack end does not stay in view between them. @Sec-memory carries spatial estimates and their uncertainty across those gaps and sets the expiry that lets the permission path refuse a claim once occlusion or age has exhausted the validated motion margin.
:::
